nodes.label: The Ḥaramayn hadith revival
nodes.full: The scholarly network of Mecca and Medina — Muḥammad Ḥayāt al-Sindī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Sayf and the successors of al-Kūrānī — pushing a return to hadith and to Ibn Taymiyya; Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's teachers.
nodes.src: background — John Voll on the Medina network; Cook (1992).

nodes.label: Ibn Taymiyya
nodes.full: The 14th-century Damascus jurist whose works, taught in Najd since the late medieval period, gave the reform its authorities and its method.
nodes.src: background — Cook, 'On the Origins of Wahhābism' (1992).

nodes.label: Urban Sunni orthodoxy
nodes.full: The established ʿulamāʾ and shrine-centred piety of the region's cities — Basra first, then the Ḥaramayn and Cairo — that condemned the movement as Kharijite extremism.
nodes.src: background — Samer Traboulsi on the early refutations.

nodes.label: The India and Egypt horse market
nodes.full: The high foreign demand — Mughal and Ottoman cavalry, Egyptian and Indian buyers — that made the Najdi mare a global luxury and a real source of interior wealth.
nodes.src: background — the ʿUqaylāt trade literature.

nodes.label: The oasis-town emirates
nodes.full: Najd stayed a patchwork of walled towns, each under an amīr from a leading family — the Muʿammar at al-ʿUyayna, the Āl Saʿūd at Dirʿiyya, the amīrs of Riyadh, Manfūḥa, Ḥuraymilāʾ, al-Majmaʿa, Buraydah and ʿUnayzah — none strong, all at feud.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd; Uwaidah al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002).

nodes.label: The Āl Saʿūd of Dirʿiyya
nodes.full: From Māniʿ al-Muraydī's settlement the family grew from holding one quarter of Dirʿiyya to holding the whole town — small amīrs among many, by the early 18th century under Saʿūd ibn Muḥammad and then Muḥammad ibn Saʿūd.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr; the Dirʿiyya dynastic tradition; Madawi Al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2010).

nodes.label: The Muʿammar of al-ʿUyayna
nodes.full: Al-ʿUyayna was for a time the strongest town of the district under the Āl Muʿammar. Its amīr ʿUthmān ibn Muʿammar first backed Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb and then, under Banū Khālid pressure, expelled him.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar; Ibn Bishr; al-Juhany (2002).

nodes.label: Banū Khālid overlordship
nodes.full: The Banū Khālid, having taken al-Aḥsāʾ from the Ottomans around 1670, made themselves the dominant power of eastern Arabia under the Āl Ḥumayd — Barrāk ibn Ghurayr, then Saʿdūn — and extended a loose, tribute-collecting suzerainty over much of Najd.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr; the Ottoman and Portuguese records of eastern Arabia; al-Juhany (2002).

nodes.label: The Ottoman and Sharifian fringe
nodes.full: The Ottomans held the Hijaz and, intermittently, al-Aḥsāʾ, but never Najd. The sharifs of Mecca claimed the Najd–Hijaz borderland and the Hajj routes and raided into the interior from time to time — the outer edge of an empire that never came in.
nodes.src: Hathaway, 'The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule' (2008); the sharifian chronicles of Mecca.

nodes.label: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, the early years
nodes.full: Born at al-ʿUyayna into a scholarly Ḥanbalī family, he studied in Medina and Basra — where his preaching against shrine practice got him expelled — and returned to Ḥuraymilāʾ, where his father was qāḍī, to write the Kitāb al-Tawḥīd.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar; Michael Cook, 'On the Origins of Wahhābism' (1992); Natana DeLong-Bas, 'Wahhabi Islam' (2004).

nodes.label: The al-ʿUyayna experiment and the expulsion
nodes.full: After his father's death he moved to al-ʿUyayna, won over its amīr, and enforced his doctrine — felling sacred trees, demolishing the tomb of Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ordering a stoning. The Banū Khālid amīr of al-Aḥsāʾ threatened Ibn Muʿammar, who expelled him.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām; Ibn Bishr; Cook (1992).

nodes.label: The pact of Dirʿiyya
nodes.full: Expelled from al-ʿUyayna, Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb was received at Dirʿiyya by its amīr Muḥammad ibn Saʿūd. The two swore a mutual oath — the amīr to protect and spread the doctrine, the shaykh to back the amīr's authority. It is the founding compact of the Saudi state.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām; Ibn Bishr; the mubāyaʿa is reconstructed from the Wahhābī chronicles. Traditionally dated 1744 (1157 AH).

nodes.label: The wars of the town emirates
nodes.full: Chronic small-scale war between the towns and their tribal allies — raids on palm groves, sieges of a few weeks, coalitions that formed and broke each season. It is the disorder the Wahhābī chroniclers would later call a return to jāhiliyya.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd, whose annals are largely a list of these campaigns; al-Juhany (2002).

nodes.label: Banū Khālid marches into Najd
nodes.full: The Āl Ḥumayd repeatedly led their tribes into the plateau to punish a town, install an amīr or collect an overdue tribute — the main external violence in Najd, and the mechanism by which they kept any one Najdi power from rising.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr; al-Juhany (2002).

nodes.label: The bedouin pressure and the bad years
nodes.full: ʿUtayba, Muṭayr, Qaḥṭān, Shammar and ʿAnaza pressed hard on the oasis districts, and a year that combined raiding with drought could empty a town. The chronicles reckon history in good and bad years as much as in reigns.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr; the poetry of Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir on the failed harvests and the raids.

nodes.label: The first acts of enforcement
nodes.full: Felling the venerated trees, demolishing the tomb at al-Jubayla and carrying out a stoning were acts of religious violence against the existing order. They made Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb too dangerous for a small-town amīr under Banū Khālid pressure to keep.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar; Cook (1992).

nodes.label: The town amirate and the majlis
nodes.full: Each town was run by its amīr through a council of the leading heads of family, with a qāḍī applying Ḥanbalī law and a militia of the townsmen. It was a workable local government — and it had no reach beyond the town wall.
nodes.src: al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002); Ibn Bishr.

nodes.label: Banū Khālid tribute and arbitration
nodes.full: The Āl Ḥumayd's suzerainty ran as tribute demands and as arbitration of the towns' quarrels — a light, extractive overlordship whose whole purpose was to stop any Najdi power from rising. That is exactly why they moved against Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr; al-Juhany (2002).

nodes.label: The oath of 1744
nodes.full: The mubāyaʿa at Dirʿiyya was a constitutional act: it defined a division of authority between a temporal ruler, the Āl Saʿūd, and a religious authority, the Āl al-Shaykh and the ʿulamāʾ, that has structured the Saudi state through all three of its foundations.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām; the analysis in Guido Steinberg, 'Religion und Staat in Saudi-Arabien' (2002).

nodes.label: The religion the reform attacked
nodes.full: Tombs, trees, caves and stones across Najd received vows and offerings — Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb at al-Jubayla, the 'male palm' of Dhū Saʿab, the cave of Bint al-Amīr, the tomb of Ḍirār. This is the practice Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb defined as shirk, associating others with God.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar (listing the sites the movement destroyed); al-Juhany (2002).

nodes.label: The Medina hadith revival
nodes.full: In the Ḥaramayn a circle of scholars — Ibrāhīm al-Kūrānī's successors, Muḥammad Ḥayāt al-Sindī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Sayf — pressed a return to hadith and to Ibn Taymiyya. Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb studied with them and took the method home.
nodes.src: John Voll, 'Muḥammad Ḥayyā al-Sindī and Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb'; Cook (1992).

nodes.label: The doctrine of tawḥīd
nodes.full: Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's core claim: the profession of God's oneness requires that every act of worship, vow, sacrifice and appeal be directed to God alone, and that seeking intercession at a tomb or a tree is idolatry that puts the person outside Islam.
nodes.src: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, Kitāb al-Tawḥīd and Kashf al-Shubuhāt; DeLong-Bas, 'Wahhabi Islam' (2004).

nodes.label: The first refutations
nodes.full: Najdi ʿulamāʾ, in the tradition his own brother Sulaymān among them, argued that the movement's charge of unbelief against ordinary Muslims was itself the error of the Kharijites. The internal Sunni argument over Wahhābism began at once and has never stopped.
nodes.src: Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, al-Ṣawāʿiq al-ilāhiyya (attribution and date debated); Cook (1992); Samer Traboulsi on the early refutations.

nodes.label: The mature Najdi town and the majlis style
nodes.full: At-Turaif at Dirʿiyya, old ʿUnayzah and Ushayqir show the developed earthen architecture — the qaṣr, the columned majlis with its triangular wall-niches and incised white plaster, the mosque with its ramp minaret — the 'Najdi style' in its classic form.
nodes.src: Geoffrey King, 'The Traditional Architecture of Saudi Arabia' (1998); the at-Turaif quarter of Dirʿiyya, a UNESCO World Heritage site (2010).

nodes.label: Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir
nodes.full: Ḥumaydān al-Shuwayʿir of al-Qaṣab was the outstanding Nabaṭī poet of pre-Saudi Najd — a satirist and moralist whose gnomic verse is a bitter, first-hand witness to the poverty, the feuding and the failure of the amīrs.
nodes.src: the dīwān of Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir; Saad Sowayan, 'Nabaṭi Poetry' (1985); P. Marcel Kurpershoek's editions and translations.

nodes.label: The amīr-poets
nodes.full: Rumayzān ibn Ghashshām of al-Ghāṭ, Jaʿaythin al-Yazīdī and other town rulers exchanged formal poems of challenge, alliance and lament. In a land with no chancery, Nabaṭī verse was the diplomatic correspondence of the emirates.
nodes.src: Kurpershoek, 'Oral Poetry and Narratives from Central Arabia'; the corpus of the early Nabaṭī amīr-poets.

nodes.label: The samir, the ʿarda and the women's song
nodes.full: The night poetry-gathering (samir), the sword-dance of the town militia (ʿarda), and the women's wedding and work songs made up the performance life that ran on under the political chaos and that the reform movement would later view with suspicion.
nodes.src: Sowayan on the samir; Lisa Urkevich, 'Music and Traditions of the Arabian Peninsula' (2015).

nodes.label: Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's writings
nodes.full: The Kitāb al-Tawḥīd, the Kashf al-Shubuhāt and the Thalāthat al-Uṣūl — short, plain, hadith-anchored texts written to teach a semi-literate society. They are still the core curriculum of the tradition he founded, in Saudi Arabia and far beyond.
nodes.src: the collected works (Muʾallafāt al-Shaykh); DeLong-Bas, 'Wahhabi Islam' (2004).

nodes.label: The Najdi town annals
nodes.full: The anonymous town chronicles and family records of 17th–18th-century Najd — dry lists of amīrs, raids, harvests and prices — are the raw material Ibn Ghannām and Ibn Bishr later worked into the first true histories of the plateau.
nodes.src: the Najdi akhbar tradition; ʿAbd Allah al-ʿUthaymin on the sources for early Najdi history.

nodes.label: The transmission of Ibn Taymiyya
nodes.full: The works of the 14th-century Damascus jurist, copied and taught in the Najdi towns since the late medieval period, gave Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb his authorities and his method. The reform was a Najdi application of an older Ḥanbalī argument, not a new one.
nodes.src: Cook, 'On the Origins of Wahhābism' (1992); the Najdi manuscript record of Ibn Taymiyya's works.

nodes.label: The date-and-khuwa economy
nodes.full: The towns lived on the date palm and paid a share of the crop as protection tribute to the dominant tribe or to Banū Khālid. The settled economy was productive but exposed — a hostage to the desert around it.
nodes.src: al-Juhany (2002); Ibn Bishr on the tribute demands.

nodes.label: The ʿUqaylāt and the horse trade
nodes.full: Najdi merchants — the ʿUqaylāt, mostly from al-Qaṣīm — drove caravans of camels and horses to Iraq, Syria and Egypt, and the trade in the Najdi mare to India through the Gulf ports made her a global luxury and a serious source of tribal and town wealth.
nodes.src: the accounts of the ʿUqaylāt trade (Musil; the later travel literature); the Indian and Egyptian demand for the Najdi horse.

nodes.label: The pastoral economy and the tribes
nodes.full: Camel and small-stock herding, the exchange of animals and transport labour with the towns, and the raid — the same structure as the medieval centuries, and no richer. The plateau's poverty is the constant of this folio.
nodes.src: al-Juhany (2002); the ethnographic literature on Najdi pastoralism.

nodes.label: Drought, famine and the fragile town
nodes.full: A run of dry years or a single lost harvest could break a town's economy and its politics at once. The Najdi chronicles measure time in years of plenty and years of hunger — sanat al-jūʿ, the year of the famine — as much as in the reigns of amīrs.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr; the famine years recorded in the Najdi annals; the poetry of Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir.

nodes.label: Well irrigation at its limit
nodes.full: The deep well and the animal-drawn bucket had reached the practical ceiling of what a Najdi town could water. Town size, and so town power, was capped by the depth of the water table and the number of wells a family could dig and man.
nodes.src: King, 'The Traditional Architecture of Saudi Arabia' (1998); al-Juhany (2002) on the demographic ceiling.

nodes.label: Firearms reach the plateau
nodes.full: The matchlock and then the flintlock spread slowly into Najd through the Gulf and Hijaz trade, changing the town siege and the raid. But powder and shot were scarce and dear, and the sword and the lance still decided most fights.
nodes.src: the arms references in Ibn Bishr; the wider history of firearms in Arabia.

nodes.label: Study in the Ḥaramayn
nodes.full: Najdi scholars went to Mecca and Medina to study and returned with books, licences and connections — the channel that brought Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb his teachers and his sources, and that also carried news of Najd out to the wider Muslim world.
nodes.src: Voll on the Medina network; Cook (1992).

nodes.label: Basra and the expulsion
nodes.full: Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's time in Basra, where he preached against local shrine practice and was driven out of the city, is the first recorded clash between his doctrine and an established urban Muslim society — a preview of every conflict that followed.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām; the biographical tradition; Cook (1992).

nodes.label: The al-Aḥsāʾ connection
nodes.full: The town emirates managed their relations with al-Aḥsāʾ constantly — tribute, appeals for arbitration, marriage, refuge. It was a Banū Khālid threat from al-Aḥsāʾ that expelled the shaykh from al-ʿUyayna and, unintentionally, sent him to Dirʿiyya.
nodes.src: Ibn Bishr; Ibn Ghannām; al-Juhany (2002).

nodes.label: The ʿUqaylāt networks abroad
nodes.full: The Qaṣīmi merchant houses kept agents and quarters in the trading cities of Iraq, Syria and Egypt — a Najdi commercial diaspora that tied the poorest interior in Arabia to the region's markets, and later reached Bombay.
nodes.src: the ʿUqaylāt trade literature; the later Najdi merchant-family histories.

nodes.label: Stateless Najd on the eve of the reform
nodes.full: A plateau of feuding oasis towns under a distant Banū Khālid overlordship, its folk religion flourishing, its poets recording the disorder — the society the Wahhābī chroniclers would portray as a new jāhiliyya, and that a revolution was about to remake.
nodes.src: al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002), which argues the pre-reform picture is partly polemical but the fragmentation real.

nodes.label: The reform as a Najdi phenomenon
nodes.full: Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's movement drew on the wider Ḥanbalī hadith revival, but its urgency, its targets — the specific trees and tombs of Najd — and its politics were local. It was a response to the condition of 18th-century Najd, not an import.
nodes.src: Cook (1992); DeLong-Bas (2004); al-Juhany (2002).

nodes.label: The thread continues — the pact and the first Saudi state
nodes.full: The folio ends with the 1744 oath at Dirʿiyya. Within sixty years the alliance of the Āl Saʿūd and the Āl al-Shaykh will have conquered most of the Arabian Peninsula and sacked the shrine cities of Iraq — the subject of the next folio.
nodes.src: a forward reference: najd-1744-1900 (the First and Second Saudi Emirates, the Egyptian destruction and the Rashīdī rivalry) is planned but not yet built.

nodes.label: The woman stoned at al-ʿUyayna
nodes.full: An early and much-cited act of the reform in power: a woman who confessed repeatedly to adultery was stoned on Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's judgement — an assertion of the ḥudūd penalties that the town emirates had largely let lapse, and a signal of what the doctrine meant in practice.
nodes.src: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar; Cook (1992).

nodes.label: Women in the emirate town
nodes.full: Closely secluded in the amīr and merchant households, more visible among the poor and the bedouin. The wedding songs, the laments and the satirical verse attributed to women are most of what survives of their voice from this period.
nodes.src: Sowayan on women's Nabaṭī poetry; al-Juhany (2002) on Najdi town society.

nodes.label: The enslaved and the freed in the towns
nodes.full: The Gulf slave trade brought enslaved Africans into the Najdi towns as farm and household labour; freedmen — the khadam — formed a recognised low stratum. The reform movement's armies would soon include both enslaved and freed soldiers.
nodes.src: Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006); the Najdi town social structure in al-Juhany (2002).
